opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is: right now, these models are incredibly smart in a raw sense, but we're using them in an extremely hobbled way. Think about what we ask of a chatbot. You give it a question, and it has to immediately start answering, essentially writing out the first thing that comes to mind, no going back, no scratchpad, no real time to think. Imagine if you had to do your job that way. Imagine you had to write a research paper or debug a big codebase where every word you wrote was final and you had about thirty seconds. You'd look pretty dumb too.

So a lot of what I mean by "unhobbling" is just removing those constraints. Give the model the ability to think for a long time, to try things, check its work, backtrack, use tools, have context on your codebase or your company the way a new employee gets onboarded over weeks. Each of those is a pretty big multiplier on effective capability, and they're often not that hard algorithmically. They're kind of low-hanging fruit.

And then reinforcement learning is the piece that gets you from imitation to actually learning on its own. Pretraining is basically learning from the internet, absorbing human text. That gets you a really strong base of knowledge and reasoning. But once you have a model that's good enough to make real attempts at hard problems, you can start doing RL on top: let it try, see whether it succeeded, reinforce what worked. That's the AlphaGo story, right? First you imitate human games, then you play against yourself and go way past humans. The analogy for language models is that once they're competent enough to produce meaningful attempts at, say, a math proof or a coding task with a verifiable outcome, they can generate their own training signal. They're not limited to what humans already wrote down.

The thing that really matters is the combination. Unhobbling gives the model the ability to work on long-horizon tasks, so instead of answering in a few seconds it's working for hours or days, like a coworker would. And RL on those long horizons teaches it how to actually use that time well: how to plan, how to notice it's going down a dead end, how to correct itself. That's the shift from a chatbot to something more like an agent, a drop-in remote worker. And once you have that, you get to a point where the models can help do AI research themselves, which is where things get really wild.

Honestly, I think people underrate this because they're looking at the chatbot interface and extrapolating from that. But the chatbot interface is the most hobbled version of the technology. The raw intelligence curve from scaling compute and algorithms is one thing, and then on top of that you have these unhobbling gains, and I think those could be just as large.

r001.rationale: The response describes pretraining as learning from internet text and compares model onboarding to a new employee, but it does not analogize human schooling to AI pretraining as preparation for independent learning.

r002.rationale: It explains that models could learn through reinforcement learning once they are competent enough, but presents this conditionally rather than claiming models are beginning to enter that regime.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, think about where we are right now. The models we have today are incredibly smart. GPT-4 can do a lot of things, but there's this weird thing where it's kind of like a brilliant intern who you can only talk to for a few minutes at a time, and then they forget everything. The models are hobbled in a bunch of really obvious ways, and I think once you un-hobble them, you get a qualitatively different thing.

So take the question of learning. Right now, the way a model learns is pretraining. You throw the whole internet at it, and it absorbs a huge amount of knowledge and a huge amount of... intuition, basically. But then it's frozen. When you actually use it, it's doing this thing where it sort of has to answer in one shot, and the only way it's "learning" within a task is the context window. That's a really bad way to learn. If I gave you a textbook and said, you have to read it once, straight through, and answer questions immediately with no notes, no going back, no trying problems, you'd do a lot worse than you actually do when you learn something.

And what humans do that's different is, you read a bit, you think about it, you try a problem, you get it wrong, you figure out why, you talk to a friend, you internalize it. That loop is the thing. It's not that humans see more data. Humans see way less data than these models. A human sees maybe a few hundred million tokens of text in a lifetime, and the models see trillions. The reason we still have this edge on sample efficiency is that we do this active, self-directed, iterative thing.

So reinforcement learning is how you get that loop. You let the model try things, you give it a signal about what worked, and it updates on that. And crucially, if you combine that with the un-hobblings, so with long context, with being able to use tools, with being able to run for hours or days on a task rather than seconds, with the model being able to check its own work and plan and so on, then you've basically turned it from this one-shot, frozen oracle into something that can actually engage with a problem the way a researcher does. It can go, okay, I don't know this, let me go read about it, let me try an experiment, that didn't work, let me think about why, let me try again.

And I think the thing people underrate is how much of the gap between the models and human experts is this stuff, rather than raw intelligence. The raw model is already very good. It's just that we're using it in this really crippled way. And the moment you give it the ability to do the loop, to learn from its own attempts on the actual task rather than only from imitation of internet text, you start to get something that improves on the job. And then you're in a very different regime, because that's the thing that lets you point it at AI research itself.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts AI pretraining with humans’ iterative, self-directed learning, but does not draw the specified analogy between human schooling and AI pretraining as preparation for independent learning.

r002.rationale: It says that combining reinforcement learning with un-hobbling lets models learn from their attempts and improve on the job, describing a move toward independent learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between a model that can answer a question and a model that can actually go off and do a task. Pretraining gives you this enormous base of knowledge and capabilities. But if you have to sit there prompting it at every step, you’re still providing a lot of the intelligence that makes the overall process work.

By unhobbling, I mean giving the model the scaffolding to use those capabilities: tools, memory, the ability to work through a problem for a long time, to run code and see what happens. If it makes a mistake, it should be able to investigate the mistake and try again, rather than just produce an answer and stop.

Reinforcement learning could then teach it to use that setup effectively. In programming, for example, it can write a solution, run tests, get feedback, and improve. You don’t need a human to write out every intermediate step. You need some way of judging whether it succeeded.

And that’s what makes independent learning plausible. The model can generate its own experience, and training can turn that experience into better capabilities. Of course, running a model in a loop doesn’t automatically mean it’s learning, and getting reliable feedback is much harder in some domains than in others. But if you can get that cycle working, you’re no longer limited to learning from examples humans have already produced.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pretraining with task execution, but it does not compare AI pretraining to human schooling.

r002.rationale: It says independent learning is plausible if a feedback cycle can be made to work; it does not claim models are beginning to enter that regime.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between a model that can answer a question in one shot and a system that can actually work on a problem. With pretraining, you learn from this enormous pile of human-generated text. But that doesn’t necessarily teach you to spend hours trying something, noticing that it failed, debugging it, and trying again.

Reinforcement learning could teach models those behaviors, especially in domains where you can check the result. In coding, for example, you can run the code and see whether the tests pass. The model can generate attempts, get feedback, and improve without a human having to write out every intermediate step.

And unhobbling is about giving the model the scaffolding to use its capabilities: tools, memory, the ability to execute code, and enough time to pursue a task. If every interaction is just a fresh context and an immediate answer, you’re constraining what it can do.

Put those together, and you could get a system that explores a problem, learns from feedback, and keeps making progress with much less human supervision. That doesn’t automatically mean it can teach itself anything—reliable feedback is a big constraint—but it opens up a much richer learning process than just imitating existing text.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pretraining on human-generated text with learning through trial and feedback, but it does not compare AI pretraining to human schooling.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning and unhobbling could enable more independent learning, but presents this as a possibility rather than claiming models are beginning to enter that regime.
